title: My family
goal: Name family members, say how old someone is, and use *tener* in all six forms.
bekal: say who is in your family
use *tener* and the expressions built on it

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Fotos en el móvil
dialogs.intro: Two classmates are waiting for class to start, and, as usual, the family photos come out.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sí, tengo una hermana y un hermano.
lines.id: Yes, I have a sister and a brother.
lines.literal: yes, I-have one sister and one brother.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: And your parents? Where do they live?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Viven en Bandung. Mi padre es profesor.
lines.id: They live in Bandung. My father's a teacher.
lines.literal: they-live in Bandung. my father is teacher.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: And your mother? Does she work too?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sí, tiene una tienda pequeña. Trabaja mucho.
lines.id: Yes, she has a small shop. She works a lot.
lines.literal: yes, she-has a shop small. works much.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: ¡Qué familia tan grande! Yo soy hija única.
lines.id: What a big family! I'm an only child.
lines.literal: what family so big! I am daughter only.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: There are five of us at home.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: And do you have any nieces or nephews?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Todavía no. Mi hermano es soltero.
lines.literal: still not. my brother is single.

notes: **Age is something you "have", not something you "are".** Spanish says *tengo veinte años* — literally "I have twenty years". *Soy veinte años* is wrong and sounds very odd. The question follows the same pattern: *¿Cuántos años tienes?* And *años* can't be dropped: *tengo veinte* on its own sounds like a sentence cut off.

**Mi, tu, su follow the NUMBER of things owned, not the owner.** One thing: *mi hermano*. More than one: *mis hermanos*. So *tus padres* doesn't mean "you all's parents", but "your parents" — plural because there are two parents.
**Su really is ambiguous.** *Su casa* can mean his house, her house, their house or your (polite) house. Spanish leaves it that way and relies on context; to be clear, people say *la casa de él*.

**The masculine plural covers mixed groups.** *Los padres* = father and mother, not "the fathers". Likewise *los hermanos* (brothers and sisters) and *los hijos* (sons and daughters, i.e. children). One woman among ten men still makes the group masculine — a grammar rule, not an opinion.
**Older or younger?** Just like English, *hermano* simply means brother. When the order matters, add a word: *mi hermano mayor* (my older brother), *mi hermano menor* (my younger brother).
**¡Qué … tan …!** A ready-made exclamation: *¡Qué familia tan grande!*, *¡Qué día tan bonito!* It also works without *tan*: *¡Qué bien!*
**Todavía no** = "not yet", a much softer answer than *no* to questions about life plans. Its opposite is *ya* ("already").

**Two forms you haven't learned yet — just recognize them.** The dialogue slips in *viven* ("they live") and *somos* ("we are"). They're the *ellos* and *nosotros* forms, covered in Units 9 and 11. For now, just know what they mean.

grammars.title: The verb tener (to have)
body: From this unit on, verb tables show **six persons**, not three as before. The new ones: *nosotros* (we), *vosotros* (you, plural) and *ellos* (they). *Usted* is in there too — the polite "you" for one person, sharing the *él / ella* row. The full system is explained in the next units — here, just recognize the forms; no need to memorize them yet.
*Tener* is irregular, but it's far too common to put off — age, family, ownership, even hunger all go through this verb:
after: *Tener* also brings a whole set of expressions where English uses "to be", not "to have": *tengo hambre* (I'm hungry), *tengo sed* (I'm thirsty), *tengo frío* (I'm cold), *tengo calor* (I'm hot), *tengo sueño* (I'm sleepy), *tengo prisa* (I'm in a hurry), *tengo miedo* (I'm scared).
One more that you'll use constantly: *tener que + verb* = "to have to". *Tengo que trabajar* — I have to work.

grammars.title: Numbers 20-100
body: Up to 29 they're written as one word; from 31 on they're separate words joined by *y*.
after: Like the number one, *veintiuno* shortens before a masculine noun: *veintiún años*. The feminine is *veintiuna*: *veintiuna personas*.
*Cien* is used for exactly one hundred; as soon as something follows, it becomes *ciento*: *cien euros* but *ciento veinte euros*. There's no *y* after *ciento* — *ciento uno*, not *ciento y uno*.

blocks.title: Family status
items: *soltero / soltera* — single · *casado / casada* — married · *divorciado / divorciada* — divorced · *viudo / viuda* — widower / widow
*hijo único / hija única* — only child · *el hermano mayor* — older brother · *el hermano menor* — younger brother · *el mayor de tres* — the oldest of three
Asking about it: *¿Estás casado?* (with *estar*, since status can change) or the more neutral *¿Tienes pareja?* ("do you have a partner?").
We have a small house in Bandung.
My grandmother is old, but she's well.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of *tener*.
items: Mi abuela ____ ochenta y siete años.

answers: Tengo dos hermanos. — ¿Cuántos años tiene tu padre? — Mi madre tiene cuarenta y cinco años. — Tenemos una casa pequeña en Bandung. — Mi abuela es mayor, pero está bien. — Tengo que trabajar.
tengo — tienes — tienen — tenemos — tiene — tenéis
veintitrés — cuarenta y ocho — sesenta — noventa y uno — cien — setenta y seis
